title: Remote Access
description: Protocols for working remotely: tunneling, encryption and VPNs (IPSec, SSL/TLS, SOCKS, SSH), remote authentication, and remote management of network devices.

nodes.title: Tunneling
nodes.description:
Encapsulating an entire packet inside the data portion of another packet. In short, adding a new header to a packet.
What tunneling allows:
- Connect private networks together across a public network such as the internet. Private IP addresses, for example 10.0 addresses, are not routable on the internet. So a packet with a private destination address is encapsulated in a packet with a public destination address.
- Carry foreign protocols over a network that does not support them, for example IPv6 packets across an IPv4 network.

children.title: GRE
children.description:
Generic Routing Encapsulation: a simple tunneling protocol that can encapsulate a wide variety of network protocols and create point-to-point connections.
It lets you easily connect two networks and pass traffic between them across a third network, typically the internet.

children.title: PPTP
children.description:
Point-to-Point Tunneling Protocol: an obsolete tunneling protocol with many well-known security vulnerabilities.
On its own, PPTP provides no encryption or authentication. It must be combined with other protocols to create VPNs.

children.title: L2TP
children.description:
Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol: the successor to PPTP, with many improvements, such as the ability to encrypt its control messages.
Very important: on its own, L2TP does not encrypt the data portion of a packet.

children.title: Split Tunneling
children.description:
Some traffic goes through the secure, encrypted tunnel, often to the corporate network, while other traffic goes straight out to the internet.
Sometimes done for performance: sending traffic straight to the internet, instead of through the tunnel first, can speed things up.
The security concern: traffic that goes straight to the internet bypasses the corporate security controls.

children.title: Encryption
children.description:
Encryption is layered on top of tunneling: encrypt the data portion of packets sent through a tunnel, to provide confidentiality.
Tunnels typically connect two private networks, or a remote device such as a laptop to a corporate network, across the public internet. Always assume that someone, probably several people, is inspecting your data as it crosses the internet.

children.title: VPN (Tunneling + Encryption)
children.description:
A Virtual Private Network is an encrypted tunnel: the data sent through the tunnel is encrypted.
The major VPN protocols to know: IPSec, SSL/TLS, SOCKS and SSH.

children.title: IPSec
children.description:
IP Security: a standardized suite of protocols that work together. The VPN protocol you need to know the most about.
It allows a massive degree of flexibility in how it is configured to create a VPN. Setting up a connection involves two choices:
- Authentication Header (AH) or Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP).
- Transport mode or Tunnel mode.
How the four combinations fit together:
- AH, transport mode: original header, AH, data. Nothing is encrypted.
- AH, tunnel mode: new header, AH, original header, data. Nothing is encrypted.
- ESP, transport mode: original header, ESP header, data, ESP trailer. The data is encrypted.
- ESP, tunnel mode: new header, ESP header, original header, data, ESP trailer. The original header and the data are encrypted.

children.title: Authentication Header
children.description:
AH provides only integrity, data-origin authentication and replay protection. No confidentiality.
Technically, IPSec in AH mode is just a tunnel, not a VPN.

children.title: Encapsulating Security Payload
children.description:
ESP provides everything AH does (integrity, data-origin authentication and replay protection) plus confidentiality, by encrypting the data portion of the payload.
IPSec in ESP mode is a VPN, because it provides an encrypted tunnel.

children.title: Transport mode
children.description: The original packet header is reused.

children.title: Tunnel Mode
children.description: A new header is created, which encapsulates the original packet header and payload.

children.title: IKE
children.description: Internet Key Exchange: the part of IPSec used to establish Security Associations.

children.title: Security Association
children.description:
A simplex (one-way) establishment of attributes for a connection, such as the authentication algorithm, the encryption algorithm and the encryption keys.
When an IPSec connection is set up, the two entities must authenticate each other (for example with X.509 digital certificates) and exchange symmetric encryption keys (for example with the Diffie-Hellman key exchange). First they must agree which authentication algorithm, encryption algorithm and IPSec mode to use. Security Associations (SAs) establish these agreements.
Simplex means an SA allows communication in one direction only:
- A tunnel where two entities talk back and forth needs 2 SAs, one for each direction.
- Adding encryption in both directions needs 2 more SAs.
A total of four SAs are required to establish an IPSec VPN.

children.title: SSL/TLS
children.description:
Another protocol commonly used to establish VPNs.
SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) was the name for the first three major versions. It was then renamed TLS (Transport Layer Security) to better reflect that it operates at layer 4, the transport layer. SSL and TLS are the same protocol; TLS is the name of the most recent versions.
Created mainly to authenticate and encrypt the connection between a web browser and a web server, but it can secure other connections too, for example a VPN.
Understand the steps to establish a TLS connection:
1. The client sends a client hello: which TLS versions and encryption algorithms it supports.
2. The server replies with a server hello, which includes a copy of the server's digital certificate.
3. The client checks the server's digital certificate, which authenticates the server: it really is Amazon.com, not sketchyhacker.com. The client then generates a new symmetric key (the session key) and encrypts it with the server's public key, taken from the certificate.
4. The client sends the encrypted session key to the server, which decrypts it with its private key. Both now have the same symmetric session key, and can efficiently encrypt all data they send back and forth.

children.title: Mutual Authentication
children.description:
In the initial client hello, the client can send its own certificate to the server, so the server can authenticate the client. The client and server then authenticate each other.
SSL/TLS can even run in a mode called unencrypted SSL, where authentication is required but an encrypted connection is not.

children.title: SOCKS
children.description:
Socket Secure protocol. Recognize it as a VPN protocol.
Operates at layer 5, the session layer.

children.title: SSH
children.description:
Secure Shell protocol. Recognize it as a VPN protocol.
Operates at layer 7, the application layer.

nodes.title: Remote Authentication
nodes.description:
Protocols to authenticate remote users, authorize them, and account for their use of a service.
Example: in 1995 you run a dial-up internet service with a few thousand customers, and need to do all three.

children.title: RADIUS
children.description:
Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service: a protocol originally designed for exactly this job.
It lets a user connect to and access network resources, and provides Authentication, Authorization and Accounting (AAA, triple A).

children.title: Diameter
children.description:
The successor to RADIUS.
Adds good security features, such as EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) for much more secure and robust authentication of users.

children.title: TACACS+
children.description:
Terminal Access Controller Access Control System Plus: does the same job as RADIUS.
The improvement: TACACS+ encrypts the full contents of the packets it sends, while RADIUS only poorly obfuscates the user's password.

nodes.title: Remote Access / Management
nodes.description:
Networks have grown ever larger, with firewalls, routers, switches and servers spread across a building, several buildings or even several countries.
These protocols let administrators connect to network devices remotely, check their status and change their configuration.

children.title: SNMP
children.description:
Simple Network Management Protocol: collects all sorts of information from network devices in real time, including performance metrics, alerts and device configuration. Beyond monitoring, it can send commands to reconfigure a device. A powerful protocol.
Memory aid: Security's Not My Problem, because the first versions are terrible for security:
- Version 1 sends passwords in clear text.
- Version 2 is a slight improvement: it allows password hashing, but not by default.
- Version 3 is a huge security improvement. If you use SNMP, use version 3.

children.title: Telnet
children.description: A protocol to connect remotely to a network device, such as a server, and get command-line interface access.
